power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Worry is common both in mental health and distress.
What, then, distinguishes pathological worry?
We hypothesized that what characterizes pathological worry is excessive internal search that fails to resolve uncertainty; i.e., is uninformative.

text.text: A 'sampling until success' heuristic was identified as a driver.
Crucially, this increase in sampling in high worriers did not increase their accuracy (CrI 100% inside ROPE), which suggests unhelpful worry.
Persistent searching-in the face of irreducible uncertainty-may therefore be a key mechanism behind worry, differentiating high from low worrying.

To explore what factors may drive sampling, binomial mixed effects models were constructed, with the dependent variable being whether the participant continued or stopped at each decision point (1 if stopped, 0 if continuing).

In this study, we showed that in an affectively inflected information-gathering task, high worriers sampled significantly more, and that within-participant, state worry was associated with increased sampling.
We show that this increased sampling in high worriers is fruitless in terms of material outcomes, as it does not increase accuracy.

In exploring what may drive increased sampling, we found that stimuli uncertainty and aversiveness increased both sampling and worry, but self-reported uncertainty predicted sampling more strongly than stimuli uncertainty.
Lastly, and importantly, we found that high worriers differ from low worriers in their response to information scarcity, sampling more persistently in information-poor environments.
Hence, our paradigm successfully operationalizes worry, as both state and trait worry are reflected in sampling.
It also shows potential to differentiate adaptive from maladaptive worry, in that persistent searching without increased success distinguished people who exhibit high, though subclinical, worry.
What drives high worriers to persist in searching, even when they are given explicit knowledge that their efforts would be less fruitful?
Our results suggest that high worry is associated with a "sampling until information found" strategy, which some participants also self-reported qualitatively.
In this strategy, participants sample until a previously unseen image is obtainedand only stop searching when this happens.
Therefore, in an information-poor environment, their sampling would naturally increase, as it takes more samples to obtain novel information.

This provides intermittent reinforcement for continuing to worry despite past unhelpfulness, and may reinforce a key positive belief about worry: that worry is endorsed as it will eventually be fruitful in problem-solving.
High trait worriers may also be less tolerant of uncertainty and are thereby compelled to continue resolving uncertainty, even when they know information is scarce.
In our task, high worriers were not more accurate despite obtaining more information.

One explanation for this is that they may not integrate information as efficiently, given the effects of worry on memory and cognition (Hayes et al., 2008; Browning et al., 2015; Goodwin et al., 2017).
text.formatted: One explanation for this is that they may not integrate information as efficiently, given the effects of worry on memory and cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Hayes et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Browning et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Goodwin et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Perceptual biases in reading facial expressions (Bradley et al., 1999; Miloff et al., 2015) may also play a role, so that high worriers may have more precise prior biases and therefore require more sensory evidence before changing their mind (because the rate of evidence accumulation decreases with prior precision).
text.formatted: Perceptual biases in reading facial expressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bradley et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Miloff et al., 2015)</ref> may also play a role, so that high worriers may have more precise prior biases and therefore require more sensory evidence before changing their mind (because the rate of evidence accumulation decreases with prior precision).

text.text: This would mean that high worriers may need more samples to reach the same standard of accuracy as low worriers.
These cognitive effects may stabilize another vicious cycle: worry increases impairment of evidence accumulation, which is compensated by worry-driven increased searching.
Stimulus aversiveness increased both sampling and self-reported worry.
This replicates studies which show attentional bias to threat in anxiety and worry (Bradley et al., 1999; Cisler & Koster, 2010; McNally, 2019).

text.text: Furthermore, changes in aversiveness over trials may be interpreted as environmental volatility, which increases information-seeking particularly in anxious individuals (Charpentier et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Furthermore, changes in aversiveness over trials may be interpreted as environmental volatility, which increases information-seeking particularly in anxious individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Charpentier et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This can be interpreted as adapting to an environment with greater implied danger.

Both stimulus uncertainty and self-reported uncertainty increased sampling and self-reported worry, aligning with theories that individuals seek information to resolve ambiguity and reduce anxiety (Carleton, 2016; Dugas et al., 2022; Vander Haegen & Etienne, 2016).
text.formatted: Both stimulus uncertainty and self-reported uncertainty increased sampling and self-reported worry, aligning with theories that individuals seek information to resolve ambiguity and reduce anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Carleton, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Dugas et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Vander Haegen & Etienne, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, the 'search until evidence' results suggest that on top of avoiding uncertainty, there may be a drive to seek signs of certainty or novelty.
The fact that sampling is 75% more likely to stop after encountering new information implies that the goal has been reached -and that novel information is rewarding or preferred.
This fits with accounts of novelty being inherently desirable (Lisman & Grace, 2005; Gottlieb et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This fits with accounts of novelty being inherently desirable <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Lisman & Grace, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Gottlieb et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Schwartenbeck et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In the context of worry and anxiety, 'search until evidence' may also function as a safety signal (Christianson et al., 2012; Seligman & Binik, 2021; Kribakaran et al., 2022; Odriozola et al., 2024), demonstrating that uncertainty reduction and safety signalling can coexist.
text.formatted: In the context of worry and anxiety, 'search until evidence' may also function as a safety signal <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Christianson et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Seligman & Binik, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Kribakaran et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Odriozola et al., 2024)</ref>, demonstrating that uncertainty reduction and safety signalling can coexist.

text.text: Hence, novel information may cause a great reduction in perceived uncertainty.
Perceived uncertainty, unlike stimuli uncertainty, is more strongly influenced by heuristics or hyperpriors, e.g. "sample until evidence" -especially under increased cognitive demand.
This aligns with dual-processing accounts, which state that people may rely on automated rule-based processing rather than more effortful assessment of precision (Evans, 2008).
text.formatted: This aligns with dual-processing accounts, which state that people may rely on automated rule-based processing rather than more effortful assessment of precision <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Evans, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, it may be the subjective, metacognitive uncertainty which underwrites worry, not informational uncertainty.
This is cleanly demonstrated by how self-reported uncertainty is a significant predictor, fully accounting for the effect of initial stimuli uncertainty.
This suggests a role for metacognition, which has been identified as a key component in models of worry (Wells, 2010; Yıldırım & Bahtiyar, 2022).
text.formatted: This suggests a role for metacognition, which has been identified as a key component in models of worry <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Wells, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Yıldırım & Bahtiyar, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, high worriers may have a metacognitive bias where their own beliefs are perceived to be less precise than they actually are, although further research should confirm this.

Nevertheless, this informs the literature of what metacognitive processes are implicated in worry (Wells, 2010; Yıldırım & Bahtiyar, 2022), providing a potential psychotherapeutic target (Jones & Menzies, 1998; Wells, 2010; Maqbool et al., 2017; Moutoussis et al., 2018), as well as suggesting a mechanistic basis for how intolerance of uncertainty may occur in worry (Bomyea et al., 2015; Vander Haegen & Etienne, 2016).

text.text: A possible limitation of the study is that findings in our population may not generalise to worry in other important, including clinical, contexts.

However, there is evidence that a continuum exists between low, typical and pathological worry, rather than their being qualitatively different (Goring & Papageorgiou, 2008), suggesting that these results may generalize.

text.text: On the other hand, findings may not generalise to populations such as adolescents or the elderly (cf. sample demographics, Table S1).
text.formatted: On the other hand, findings may not generalise to populations such as adolescents or the elderly (cf. sample demographics, Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: Our results offer an important hypothesis regarding the metacognitive beliefs that may sustain worry.
Positive beliefs that worry is helpful increase worry (Davey, 2008; Hebert et al., 2014; Wells, 2006), and targeting these beliefs can reduce worry (Laberge et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Positive beliefs that worry is helpful increase worry <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Davey, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Hebert et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Wells, 2006)</ref>, and targeting these beliefs can reduce worry <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Laberge et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: The present work suggests a specific positive metacognitive belief: lack of success means 'I am on the right path, I have not searched enough', not 'I should stop worrying'.

Such metacognitive aspects of beliefs can constitute a useful target for metacognitive therapy (Hepworth et al., 2013; Wells, 2010) or indeed cognitive behavioural and related therapies, wherein beliefs are explicitly examined and modified (Moutoussis et al., 2018; Nair et al., 2020).

text.text: Worry being driven by uninformative searching has implications in today's informationoverloaded world.

While we can access a vast amount of information, much of it is low-quality, and AI-generated and AI-amplified misinformation is widespread (Arnold et al., 2023; Monteith et al., 2024; Saeidnia et al., 2025).
text.formatted: While we can access a vast amount of information, much of it is low-quality, and AI-generated and AI-amplified misinformation is widespread <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arnold et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Monteith et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Saeidnia et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Even search engines are perceived to be worsening (Bevendorff et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Even search engines are perceived to be worsening <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bevendorff et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, while today's world may seem information-rich, the reality is that it is information-poor, requiring sifting through much poor-quality information before useful knowledge is obtained; paralleling the design of this experiment.
As such, it is important that this paradigm defines failure in sampling not as getting no data, but getting uninformative data.

Given that we have shown that information scarcity increases worry-like behaviour in the form of unfruitful information sampling, especially in high worriers, this provides a potential mechanism behind the digital world amplifying worry.

And worry causing particular patterns of digital activity e.g. 'doomscrolling' (Buchanan et al., 2021; Rajeshwari & Meenakshi, 2023; Türk-Kurtça & Kocatürk, 2025), causing vicious cycles (Alsaigh et al., 2022; Elhai et al., 2025).
text.formatted: And worry causing particular patterns of digital activity e.g. 'doomscrolling' <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Buchanan et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Rajeshwari & Meenakshi, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Türk-Kurtça & Kocatürk, 2025)</ref>, causing vicious cycles <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alsaigh et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Elhai et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Assessing worry through over-sampling may also become useful in the ecological monitoring of mental states.
Everyday interactions often involve information search, e.g., checking email inboxes and other media.

Understanding this naturally occurring sampling with respect to worry could allow them to be evaluated as markers of mental states, providing information seamlessly without actions being interrupted (as self-reporting requires).
This could be done via system integration into software, akin to wearable technologies providing monitoring of mental health (Morris & Aguilera, 2012; Yen, 2021).
text.formatted: This could be done via system integration into software, akin to wearable technologies providing monitoring of mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Morris & Aguilera, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Yen, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This has potential in tracking signs of mental distress in disorders where a worsening trend could be reflected by an increase in worry, such as GAD or OCD.

This would also help studying the brain as a dynamic system, which may have attributes such as early warning signs for mental decompensation (Cui et al., 2025; Dablander et al., 2023), as being able to quantify worry or worry-like behaviour allows a look into what is 'under the hood'.

text.text: However, such seamless monitoring requires very careful ethical and regulatory measures, to protect subjects with respect to their privacy and data rights, and even unintended consequences such as worries about being monitored.
It may mean monitoring fully controlled by the user themselves in collaboration with trusted clinicians, in a self-empowering way, akin to integrating assistive technology into daily life.
This paper makes several key contributions.

It provides an account of worry as sampling information, not just semantic, e.g., health or climate change information (Diefenbach et al., 2001; Bouman et al., 2020; Seiter & Brophy, 2020; Ojala et al., 2021), but sensory and affective information.
text.formatted: It provides an account of worry as sampling information, not just semantic, e.g., health or climate change information <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Diefenbach et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bouman et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Seiter & Brophy, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Ojala et al., 2021)</ref>, but sensory and affective information.

text.text: This gracefully accommodates both cognitive and affective phenomena in worry.
Second, the paper clarifies moment-to-moment fluctuations in worry, such as when participants respond to environmental changes (e.g. changes in information availability).

This allows for the phenomenology of worry, and specifically its metacognitive dimension to be captured as it fluctuates over time, complementing static measures of worry tendency captured by questionnaires.

Lastly, it answers key questions about the difference between healthy worry and maladaptive, unhelpful worry; providing a clean, mechanism-based way to differentiate them for the benefit of mental health and society.

text.text: This created a context in which uncertainty about another person's feelings had meaningful consequences, reflecting the kind of emotional ambiguity that can trigger worry in everyday life.
This is ecologically valid as having to navigate emotional uncertainty is stressful and commonly experienced.
This would naturally correspond with worries such as "is he mad at me?"
and "what if they are in a bad mood when I get home?".

Worries about other people's feelings often occur (Borkovec, 1985; Diefenbach et al., 2001; Roemer et al., 1997), and sometimes even involve imagining their facial expression (Szabó & Lovibond, 2002).

text.text: Then, importantly, participants could sample additional facial expressions by pressing a key.

Most sampling attempts simply repeated already seen facial expressions, but there is a chance of revealing a new expression: either 1 to 5 (information rich environment) or 1 to 40 (information poor environment).
This new expression is outlined in green.

This sampling phase allowed participants to gather more information before making a final judgment, mirroring the tendency to keep mentally revisiting a socially uncertain situation when concerned about possible negative outcomes.
When they felt ready, participants pressed enter to declare their final emotion read, confidence estimate, and worry about the scream ('how worried are you about a possible scream?').
At the end of each trial, if their final rating was inaccurate by more than one unit, there was a 50% chance that a scream would be played.
Participants completed 32 trials in total.

High worry is associated with a 'sample until success' approach.
